justification: Re-judged fresh against the current top results for 'process vs thread': ByteByteGo (a five-bullet comparison list, no code, no measurements, no primary-source citations, a context-switch mention with no mechanism or numbers) and GeeksforGeeks (definitions plus a comparison table, two unlabelled stock diagrams, no runnable code, no citations to academic or vendor primary sources). This article remains a different class of page on value-add alone: six original, verified C# programs, two captioned diagrams with accessible title/desc, four varied exercises with worked solutions (explain-a-mechanism, find-the-bug, measure-it, apply-a-decision -- not a repeated 'predict the output' template), and a sources list of primary documentation, man pages, runtime source and a peer-reviewed measurement paper, all cited inline at the point of the claim they support. Headings and exercise titles are specific to this content, not boilerplate. Structure still reads as its own shape (a C-shaped comparison/decision guide), not a template copy of neighbouring pillar articles. docs/crosslinks/operating-systems/processes-and-threads.md still exists and still scopes the article away from near-duplicate coverage of the race-condition, scheduling, virtual-memory and async/await siblings, so missing in-body links to those unpublished articles are correctly not penalized. This round's primary job was to re-check the three round-1 copying findings against the actual source pages, sentence by sentence, rather than trust that the wording had merely changed. Two of the three are genuinely fixed, not cosmetically: (1) the Chromium sentence no longer tracks the source's clause order or vocabulary -- 'treat occasional crashes and hangs in that code as a given to design around, not a bug backlog to clear before shipping' is a different sentence built on a different (backlog) metaphor, and a web search for the distinctive Chromium phrase and for the article's own new phrasing found no match to either the source or any third-party page; (2) the process/thread attribute paragraph now genuinely regroups the Microsoft Learn enumeration under the writer's own 'identity vs. resource' distinction, with the items inside each group reordered relative to the source, not just re-verbed in place; (3) the context-switch mechanism paragraph now leads with the scheduling decision (which thread runs next) before the bookkeeping (save/requeue/restore), reversing the source's numbered-list order and adding explanatory framing the source doesn't have, so it can no longer be reconstructed by lining it up against Microsoft's four bullets. However, being skeptical of a cosmetic fix paid off on a fourth spot: the very next paragraph in the same 'What a context switch costs' section, the sentence beginning 'A switch happens when a thread's time slice (its quantum) runs out...', was not touched, and it has the identical defect round 1 flagged elsewhere in this section -- see the issue below. Because one hard-rule 'never closely paraphrase' violation is still live in the section that was the whole point of this round, the score cannot reach the 8.5 'equal to MDN/Real Python, only nits' band, but it is meaningfully ahead of round 1 (which had a blocker plus two majors) now that the blocker and two of the three findings are real, structural fixes rather than synonym swaps.

issues.location: Section 'What a context switch costs', second paragraph, sentence beginning "A switch happens when a thread's time slice (its quantum) runs out and an equal-priority thread is ready, when a higher-priority thread becomes ready, or when the running thread has to wait for something, in which case it gives up the rest of its slice ([Context Switches])."
issues.problem: This three-item enumeration reproduces the exact order and structure of Microsoft Learn's 'Context Switches' page's 'most common reasons for a context switch' list -- '(1) The quantum of a thread expired, and another thread with at least the same priority is ready; (2) A thread with a higher priority has become ready to run; (3) A running thread needs to wait' plus its trailing sentence 'When a running thread needs to wait, it relinquishes the remainder of its time slice' -- with a near-synonym substituted for almost every clause (expired -> runs out; at least the same priority -> equal-priority, dropping the 'at least' nuance; has become ready to run -> becomes ready; needs to wait -> has to wait for something; relinquishes the remainder of its time slice -> gives up the rest of its slice) while 'is ready' survives verbatim. This is the same patchwriting pattern the round-1 blocker and majors were about, present in the same section, immediately after the sentence that WAS genuinely rewritten (the preceding 'decision wrapped in bookkeeping' paragraph). It reads as transcribed-with-a-thesaurus, not restated from understanding.
issues.fixLooksLike: Don't enumerate the three triggers in the source's order with parallel wording. For example, group by who initiates the switch -- the running thread gives it up voluntarily (waiting) versus the scheduler takes it away (quantum expiry or a higher-priority arrival) -- and state the 'at least the same priority' nuance precisely (a same-or-higher-priority thread becoming ready also ends the quantum early) instead of narrowing it to 'equal-priority', since the narrowed claim is also less accurate than the source.
